title: Andes Technology has shut down Condor Computing.
gist: Andes Technology has reportedly shut down Condor Computing, the Austin subsidiary it founded in March 2023 to build the out-of-order 64-bit RISC-V 'Cuzco' CPU IP for data-center, AI and HPC workloads; the report rests on a single industry publication (Jon Peddie Research) with no official Andes confirmation and no clarity on Cuzco's designs and patents.

themes.theme: Condor shutdown and unresolved Cuzco IP

insights.claim: Andes Technology has reportedly shut down its Austin-based subsidiary Condor Computing as of August 13, 2026, ending it as an operating unit.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A dated shutdown of a high-performance RISC-V effort is a concrete data point against the near-term data-center RISC-V thesis.
insights.quote: As of August 13, 2026, Andes Technology has reportedly shut down its Austin-based subsidiary, Condor Computing.

insights.claim: What Andes will do with Cuzco's designs and patents has not been publicly clarified, leaving valuable out-of-order RISC-V microarchitecture IP in limbo.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Orphaned out-of-order RISC-V IP and its engineering team are an acquisition target — watch for asset purchases by RISC-V or hyperscaler buyers.
insights.quote: what Andes will do with Cuzco’s designs and patents has not yet been publicly clarified
insights.locator: The shutdown appears to end Condor

insights.claim: The shutdown report comes from a single industry publication, Jon Peddie Research, with no official Andes announcement located, so the news carries single-source risk.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Size any trade on this as unconfirmed until Andes files or announces; the sourcing caveat is explicit in the report itself.
insights.quote: The report is currently from a single industry publication, with no official Andes announcement located yet.
insights.locator: The shutdown appears to end Condor

themes.theme: What Condor was built to do

insights.claim: Andes established Condor Computing in March 2023 as a wholly owned US R&D subsidiary to extend its American presence and give a specialized team responsibility for advanced CPU cores.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Roughly three years from founding to shutdown sets a realistic time-to-failure benchmark for high-performance CPU IP ventures.
insights.locator: Condor Computing is an Austin, Texas–based

insights.claim: Cuzco is a 64-bit RISC-V design using out-of-order execution and patented microarchitectural techniques aimed at data-center, AI, automotive and HPC workloads with better performance per watt and area efficiency.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Defines what capability just left the market: licensable high-end out-of-order RISC-V, narrowing options for SoC teams seeking an Arm alternative.

insights.claim: Condor sold licensable CPU designs rather than complete chips, letting chipmakers customize products without building a core from scratch — the same IP-licensing model as its competitors.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: IP licensing has low revenue visibility until design wins convert; the model's cash-burn profile explains why sub-scale entrants get shut.
insights.quote: Rather than manufacturing complete chips, Condor develops licensable CPU designs that customers can integrate into their own systems-on-chip.

themes.theme: RISC-V versus Arm and x86 in high performance

insights.claim: Cuzco was part of a broader industry effort to push RISC-V beyond embedded and low-power devices into markets historically dominated by Arm and x86 — an effort this shutdown sets back.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Fewer credible high-performance RISC-V cores extends Arm's and x86's incumbency in servers — mildly supportive for Arm's royalty runway.
insights.quote: Cuzco reflects a broader industry effort to expand RISC-V beyond embedded and low-power devices into markets historically dominated by proprietary architectures such as Arm and x86.
